one_liner: Header-only C++11 work-stealing scheduler storing task objects inside its deques; lower spawn overhead than TBB 4.3 and Cilk Plus.
what_it_does: A minimal fork-join task scheduler: you derive a class from staccato::task<T> with a void execute() method, placement-new children into memory returned by child(), call spawn() on each and wait() for them. A scheduler<T>(max_subtasks, nthreads) object owns the worker threads and runs a root task via root()/spawn()/wait(). There is no parallel_for, futures or heterogeneous task types: one scheduler serves one task type T.
how_it_is_fast: Instead of a Chase-Lev deque of task pointers, each worker keeps a chain of fixed-size task_deque arrays (one per task-graph level) that hold the task objects themselves, so spawning a task never calls the heap allocator and finished slots are reused in LIFO order. Per-worker memory comes from a bump-style lifo_allocator with no thread safety or fragmentation handling, keeping tasks contiguous; the README shows fewer LLC misses than TBB and Cilk Plus. The deque uses relaxed atomics with explicit fences (top/bottom/nstolen counters) so it is valid on weak memory models.
when_to_use: Recursive divide-and-conquer with tiny tasks (fib, tree search, recursive sums) where scheduler overhead dominates, which is where its fib(42) and dfs 9^9 charts show the gap over TBB and Cilk Plus.
Task graphs whose maximum fan-out per task is known at compile or design time (for example 2 for binary recursion).
As a small, readable reference implementation of a task-object-storing work-stealing deque to study or vendor.
Projects stuck on C++11 that want a dependency-free header drop.
when_not_to_use: Memory-bound kernels (matmul, block matmul): the README says the gain there is negligible.
Irregular task graphs with unbounded or data-dependent fan-out: you must fix the maximum subtasks per task up front.
Production code needing parallel algorithms, futures, cancellation, exceptions across tasks or mixed task types: only spawn/wait on one type T exists; use oneTBB, Taskflow or libfork instead.
Anything needing maintenance: last commit 2018-06-13; open issues include the matmul benchmark consuming 128 GB+ of memory (#4) and benchmark crashes on atoi (#3), both unanswered.
Latency-sensitive or shared machines: idle workers spin in a steal loop calling std::this_thread::yield() rather than sleeping.

integration.platforms: any platform with C++11 threads and atomics; benchmarked only on x86-64 Linux
integration.thread_safety: Scheduler is driven from one master thread (root()/spawn()/wait()); spawn/wait inside execute() are per-worker; not documented beyond that

gotchas: Not truly header-only for multi-file builds: include/lifo_allocator.hpp defines non-template, non-inline member functions (lifo_allocator::page::set_next, page::alloc, lifo_allocator::alloc, inc_tail and others) at namespace scope, so including the scheduler from two translation units gives duplicate-symbol link errors unless you patch in 'inline'.
Tasks must be constructed with placement new over child()/root() memory; allocating them any other way breaks the scheduler's memory model.
The scheduler(degree, nthreads, height) constructor rounds degree up to a power of two and preallocates per-level deques; exceeding the declared fan-out is not checked in release builds.
The TBB comparison uses blocking-style TBB tasks (wait_for_all) without continuation passing or scheduler bypass; issue #1 notes TBB's gap would shrink with those.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over Nowa or Heartbeat Scheduling only when you want a tiny dependency-free C++11 header to study or vendor for fixed-fan-out recursion; for maintained, general-purpose work stealing citor, Fork Union or Taskflow-class libraries are safer, and Weave (Nim) reports similar overhead wins over TBB with more benchmarks.
verified_claims_summary: On two Xeon E5 v4 sockets (14 cores each, 56 threads), g++ 7.2.1 -O3, Linux 4.13, the README charts show fib(42) at 56 threads about 1.6x faster than Intel Cilk Plus 7.3 and 2.4x faster than TBB 4.3, and dfs 9^9 about 2.5x and 3.4x faster (ratios read off log-scale PNG charts by the verifier, approximate), with matmul and blkmul nearly unchanged. The checked-in benchmarks/run.sh is left in a debug state (2 runs at 3-4 threads, only staccato fib enabled), so the published charts used settings that the script no longer runs by default.
status_note: Abandoned since 2018 (37 stars, four open issues with no replies) but MIT-licensed and only about 950 lines of headers, so it is easy to vendor after adding 'inline' to the lifo_allocator definitions.
